debrief.whyItWorks: When most positions are unknown and the clock is long, information converts the execute from a guess into a read. Here, 5 players faced 4 with about 74 seconds left.
debrief.cost: It spends round clock, which limits the later options.
debrief.assumption: There is enough clock left to act on whatever the information shows.
debrief.breaksWhen: The clock runs down before the information is used, so the team has to execute blind anyway.

evidenceReview.explanation: Three defenders could not be placed. Unaccounted-for opponents are the main risk to any committed plan and the main reason to gather information.
The round clock stood near 74 seconds. The round clock bounds how long any plan can take.
It was 5 players against 4. The head count sets how many duels the team can lose and still carry out its plan.
The confirmed position of one defender in Middle was current. A sighting narrows where contact is likely, but its value falls quickly with age.
The team had one smoke and five flashes and no HE grenades or molotovs. The utility left sets how much of the plan can be forced rather than hoped for.

debrief.followupReview: The follow-up was judged against the line you locked. The update made another line stronger, so even a sound first call did best to move: "Execute on the site now". Changing course earned the value of the new line less the time and position a switch costs, so correcting a weaker call still scored well, while abandoning a sound one or holding on to a weak one did not.
debrief.strongestAlternative: The closest alternative was to fake one site and rotate, spending clock and utility to pull defenders out of position.

counterfactual.changedFact: The round clock is under half a minute.
counterfactual.effect: Gathering information no longer fits, and committing at once becomes stronger.
